To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
left subclavian revascularization in thoracic endovacular repair is associated with decreased stroke rate.
coverage of the left subclavan artery (LSA), without revascularization, in thoracic endovacular aortic repair is a risk factor for stroke and possibly for spinal cord injury.
left subclavian coverage with revascularisation is associated with a lower risk of stroke and spinal cord injury.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the left subclavan artery revascularization during zone 2 TEVR.
the management of the LSA in zone 2 TEAVR.
the best management strategy for LSA in zone 2 TEAR.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the best strategy for LSA management in pathologic processes requiring zone 2 TEVR is to revascularize the LSA.
the best management strategy for LSA in zone 2 TEVR remains controversial, and further prospective studies are needed.
revascularization of the LSA is recommended to reduce the risk of stroke, but not SCI, in zone 2 TEAVR.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LSA should be revascularized in zone 2 TEVR, but that there is no difference in stroke risk with synchronous vs metachronous revascularization.
revascularization of the LSA in zone 2 TEVR is associated with lower risk of stroke, and this is true for all aortic diseases and regardless of when the LSA is revascularized.

LSA revascularizations should be performed in zone 2 TEVR, with a lower threshold to revascularize the LSA in patients with atherosclerotic aortic disease and a higher threshold for patients with acute aortic dissection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LSA revascularizations are safe and should be performed in zone 2 TEAVR.
LSA revascularizations should be performed in all patients undergoing TEVAR, with the best timing being synchronous with TEVAR.
LSA coverage without intervention is associated with an increased risk of stroke.
